objectives: Explain which EM waves are used for communication and why
Describe how radio waves are produced and detected (HT)
Explain the dangers of UV, X-rays and gamma rays and use radiation dose

questions.q: Name the EM wave with the highest frequency.
questions.a: Gamma rays.

questions.q: State two properties shared by all EM waves.
questions.a: Any two: transverse; travel at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s in a vacuum; transfer energy; travel through a vacuum.

questions.q: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz. Calculate its wavelength. (c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s)
What happens to the speed of light when it passes from air into glass?
questions.a: It slows down.

questions.q: Name the EM wave detected by a thermal imaging camera.
questions.a: Infrared.

questions.q: What is an ion?
questions.a: An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it has a charge.

engage.hook: Since 2011 it has been illegal for under-18s to use a sunbed in England. Why ban something that just gives you a tan?
engage.imageDescription: open tanning sunbed with blue UV tubes glowing

reveal.answer: Sunbeds give out ultraviolet. UV can damage the DNA in skin cells, ageing the skin early and raising the risk of skin cancer. Young skin is most at risk.

learn.heading: EM waves for communication

items: Long-wave radio diffracts around the curved Earth, so it reaches places out of sight of the transmitter.
Short-wave radio reflects off the ionosphere, a charged layer high in the atmosphere.
Microwaves pass through the ionosphere, so they carry signals to and from satellites.
Infrared: TV remote controls. Visible light: fibre optic broadband.

learn.imageDescription: diagram of the Earth showing radio waves reflecting off the ionosphere and microwaves passing through to a satellite

steps.label: Wave reaches receiver
steps.note: the fields make its electrons oscillate

steps.label: AC induced
steps.note: same frequency as the radio wave

learn.heading: Where EM waves come from

items: An electron that absorbs energy jumps to a higher energy level.
When it drops back, it emits an EM wave, often visible light or UV.
Gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
The nucleus loses energy as the gamma ray is emitted.

learn.imageDescription: Bohr model of a hydrogen atom with an electron moving between energy levels

learn.heading: Dangers and radiation dose

items: UV: skin ages early and the risk of skin cancer rises.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising: they can mutate genes and cause cancer.
The higher the frequency, the more energy each wave carries.
Dose (in sieverts, Sv) measures the risk of harm. 1 Sv = 1000 mSv.
Chest X-ray 0.1 mSv. CT scan 10 mSv. 100 mSv gives a small rise in cancer risk.

learn.imageDescription: flow from ionising radiation to DNA mutation to cancer cells and tumour

build.q: Which EM wave is used to send signals to and from satellites?
build.explanation: Microwaves pass through the ionosphere. Many radio waves are reflected by it.

build.q: Why can long-wave radio be picked up far beyond the horizon?
options: It diffracts around the curved Earth
build.explanation: Long wavelengths diffract around the curve of the Earth.

build.q: A transmitter is supplied with 200 kHz alternating current. What is the frequency of the current induced in the receiver?
build.explanation: The induced current has the same frequency as the radio wave and the original current.

build.q: Which change produces gamma rays?
options: A change in the nucleus of an atom
An electron dropping to a lower energy level
An electron rising to a higher energy level
build.explanation: Gamma rays come from the nucleus. Electron changes give visible light and UV.

build.q: Which type of EM radiation can make skin age early?
build.explanation: UV damages skin cells: early ageing and a higher risk of skin cancer.

build.q: What does a radiation dose in sieverts measure?
options: The risk of harm from the radiation
The number of waves each second
build.explanation: Dose measures the risk of harm to the body from an exposure.

worked.prompt: How many chest X-rays (0.1 mSv each) give the same dose as one CT scan (10 mSv)?
steps: Divide the bigger dose by the smaller dose.

yourTurn.prompt: Natural sources give 0.012 mSv per day. How many days give the same dose as a 0.18 mSv X-ray?

statements.text: Mobile phone microwaves are ionising, like X-rays.
statements.correction: Microwaves are low frequency and not ionising. Only high-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma ionise.

statements.text: Radio waves travel more slowly than gamma rays in a vacuum.
statements.correction: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.

statements.text: A bigger dose in sieverts means a bigger risk of harm.
Gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus.
A small dose of X-rays carries no risk at all.
statements.correction: Any dose carries some risk. A small dose means a small risk.

developing.q: Name the EM wave used for: (a) a TV remote, (b) satellite TV, (c) fibre optic broadband.
Give two harmful effects of ultraviolet on skin.
developing.a: Skin ages early. Higher risk of skin cancer.

developing.q: Where do gamma rays come from?
developing.a: Changes in the nucleus of an atom.

reaching.q: Explain why microwaves, not radio waves, are used to communicate with satellites.
reaching.a: Microwaves pass through the ionosphere to reach the satellite. Many radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere.

reaching.q: Explain how X-rays can cause cancer.
reaching.a: X-rays are ionising. They can damage DNA and mutate genes. Mutated cells can divide out of control and form a tumour.

reaching.q: A CT scan gives 10 mSv. A chest X-ray gives 0.1 mSv. How many chest X-rays give the same dose as one CT scan?

mastering.q: (HT) Describe how a radio wave is sent from a transmitter and detected by a receiver.
mastering.a: AC makes electrons oscillate in the transmitter, emitting a radio wave. In the receiver it makes electrons oscillate, inducing AC of the same frequency.

mastering.q: Natural sources give 0.012 mSv per day. How many days give the same dose as a 0.18 mSv X-ray?
A flight attendant gets 1.7 mSv a year from flying. 100 mSv gives a small cancer risk. Should they worry? Explain.
mastering.a: Not much: 1.7 mSv is about 60 times below 100 mSv. But any dose carries some risk, and it adds up over a career.

objectives: Explain what coherent sources are and why interference needs them
Link maxima and minima to path difference and phase difference
Describe two-source interference with sound and microwaves

questions.q: State the principle of superposition.
questions.a: When waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.

questions.q: Two waves are 180° out of phase. Give this phase difference in radians.
questions.a: π rad

questions.q: The amplitude of a wave halves. What happens to its intensity?
questions.a: It falls to a quarter (I \propto A^2).

questions.q: Calculate the wavelength of a 2.0 kHz sound wave in air. (v = 340 m s^-1)
State the two conditions for total internal reflection.
questions.a: Light travels towards a lower refractive index; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

questions.q: Name the wave behaviour that only transverse waves show.
questions.a: Polarisation.

engage.hook: Two speakers play the same note. Walk across the field in front of the stage. What do you hear?
engage.imageDescription: outdoor festival stage with two large speaker stacks either side
engage.prompt: Where is the best place to stand, and why?

learn.heading: Coherent sources

items: Coherent waves have a constant phase difference.
To be coherent they must have the same frequency.
Only coherent sources give a steady interference pattern.
Two speakers driven by one signal generator.
One microwave transmitter shining through two slits.
One laser lighting two slits. Two separate lamps are never coherent.

learn.imageDescription: incoherent waves with changing phase above coherent waves with constant phase difference

learn.heading: Path difference and phase difference

items: Path difference = nλ (0, λ, 2λ ...).
Phase difference = 0, 2π, 4π ... The waves arrive in phase.
Path difference = (n + ½)λ (½λ, 1½λ ...).
Phase difference = π, 3π, 5π ... The waves arrive in antiphase.

learn.imageDescription: two sources with waves meeting at points A to F, labelled with path difference 0, half wavelength and 2 wavelengths

learn.heading: Two-source interference patterns

items: Two speakers on one signal generator.
Walking parallel to them you hear loud (maxima) and quiet (minima) regions in turn.
A transmitter, a metal sheet with two slits and a probe receiver.
Moving the probe gives a pattern of maxima and minima. Central maximum: path difference 0.

learn.imageDescription: two-source interference pattern with lines of maxima and minima labelled with path and phase difference

build.q: What does it mean for two wave sources to be coherent?
options: They have a constant phase difference
build.explanation: Coherent: constant phase difference, which needs the same frequency. The phase difference need not be zero.

build.q: The path difference at a point is 2.5λ. What is the phase difference?
build.explanation: Phase difference = 2π × path difference ÷ λ = 2π × 2.5 = 5π rad.

build.q: Two coherent waves meet with a phase difference of 3π rad. What is observed?
build.explanation: An odd multiple of π means antiphase, so destructive interference: a minimum.

build.q: Why do two separate lamps not give a visible interference pattern?
build.explanation: Separate lamps are not coherent: the phase difference changes randomly, so the pattern averages out.

build.q: Two speakers emit 680 Hz sound. v = 340 m s^-1. What is the path difference at the first minimum?
build.explanation: λ = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m. First minimum: path difference ½λ = 0.25 m.

build.q: A microwave probe moves from the central maximum to the next maximum. How does the path difference change?
build.explanation: Central maximum: 0. First-order maximum: λ.

worked.prompt: Two speakers share one signal generator. At the first-order maximum the path difference is 0.28 m. v = 340 m s^-1. Find the frequency.
steps: First-order maximum: path difference = λ, so λ = 0.28 m

yourTurn.prompt: Coherent sound of frequency 2.0 kHz, v = 340 m s^-1. Find the path difference at the second-order minimum.

statements.text: Destructive interference destroys the energy of the waves.
statements.correction: Energy is redistributed: less at the minima, more at the maxima.

statements.text: Coherent waves must have the same amplitude.
statements.correction: Coherent means same frequency and constant phase difference. Equal amplitudes just give zero at the minima.

statements.text: At the central maximum the path difference is zero.
A path difference of 2.5λ gives a minimum.
Microwaves cannot show interference because they are invisible.
statements.correction: All waves interfere. A probe receiver detects the microwave maxima and minima.

developing.q: State the conditions needed to see a steady two-source interference pattern.
developing.a: The sources must be coherent: the same frequency and a constant phase difference.

developing.q: State the path difference for constructive and for destructive interference.
Give the phase difference, in radians, at the second-order minimum and at the second-order maximum.
developing.a: Second-order minimum: 3π rad. Second-order maximum: 4π rad.

reaching.q: Two dippers make coherent water waves. The path difference to the second-order maximum is 9.0 cm. Find the wavelength.
Explain why the sound is quieter at some points between two speakers.
reaching.a: Waves arrive in antiphase, path difference (n + ½)λ. By superposition the displacements cancel: destructive interference, a minimum.

reaching.q: Speakers emit 1.7 kHz sound. v = 340 m s^-1. Find the path difference at the first-order maximum.
reaching.a: λ = 340 ÷ 1700 = 0.20 m. First-order maximum: path difference = λ = 0.20 m

mastering.q: Sound of 2.0 kHz, v = 340 m s^-1. Find the path difference that gives a phase difference of 5π rad.
mastering.a: λ = 0.17 m. 5π rad = 2.5λ, so path difference = 2.5 × 0.17 = 0.43 m

mastering.q: A microphone moves along a line parallel to two speakers. Explain the pattern it detects.
mastering.a: Alternate maxima and minima. Maxima: path difference nλ, in phase, constructive. Minima: (n + ½)λ, antiphase, destructive.

mastering.q: Noise-cancelling headphones make sound that cancels engine noise. Suggest the phase and amplitude of that sound.
mastering.a: In antiphase with the noise (phase difference π) and the same amplitude, so superposition gives almost zero displacement.

objectives: Describe how pressure in a liquid changes with depth
Explain why pressure increases with depth
Plot and use a graph of pressure against depth

questions.q: Write the equation for pressure.
questions.a: pressure = force ÷ area

questions.q: A box pushes down with 600 N on an area of 2 m^2. Calculate the pressure.
Why does a sharp knife cut more easily than a blunt one?
questions.a: The sharp edge has a small area, so the same force gives a bigger pressure.

questions.q: Why is air pressure lower at the top of a mountain?
questions.a: There is less air above you, so less weight of air pushes down.

questions.q: Describe how the particles are arranged in a liquid.
questions.a: Close together, in a random arrangement, and able to move past each other.

questions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
questions.a: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

engage.hook: Divers who go hundreds of metres down wear a hard metal suit like this. What is it protecting them from?
engage.imageDescription: atmospheric diving suit being lowered into the sea

reveal.answer: The pressure of the water above them. Every 10 m of sea water adds about as much pressure as the whole atmosphere pressing on you.

learn.heading: Pressure in liquids

items: Liquid particles hit every surface they touch.
Each collision pushes on the surface.
Liquid pressure acts in all directions.
Deeper down, there is more liquid above you.
The weight of that liquid pushes down on the liquid below.
So the pressure increases with depth.

learn.imageDescription: beach ball being pushed deeper under water and getting squashed from all sides

learn.heading: Living and building with water pressure

items: Depth: deeper water gives more pressure.
Density: a denser liquid gives more pressure at the same depth.
The shape of the container does not matter.
Dams are built thickest at the bottom.
Divers' ears hurt more the deeper they go.
Deep-sea animals are adapted to huge pressures.

learn.imageDescription: cross-section of a dam wall that is much thicker at the bottom than the top

build.q: What happens to the pressure in water as you go deeper?
build.explanation: There is more water above you, so the pressure increases.

build.q: Why does water pressure increase with depth?
options: The water is warmer deeper down
More water is above, pushing down
The particles are bigger deeper down
There is less air above the water
build.explanation: The weight of the water above pushes down on the water below.

build.q: A beach ball is pushed deeper under water. What happens to it?
options: It is squashed from all sides
It is squashed from the top only
build.explanation: Water pressure acts in all directions and gets bigger with depth.

build.q: In which direction does water pressure push on a submarine?
build.explanation: Particles hit the hull from every side, so the pressure acts in all directions.

build.q: The sea pressure is 100 atmospheres at 1000 m deep. What is it at 3000 m?
build.explanation: Three times as deep gives three times the pressure from the water.

build.q: Which dam design is best?
options: The same thickness all the way
build.explanation: Water pressure is biggest at the bottom, so the wall must be strongest there.

build.setup: A tall can has three holes, one above the other. It is filled with water.
build.prediction: Which hole squirts water the furthest?
build.reveal: The bottom hole. Its jet goes furthest.
build.explanation: The bottom hole has the most water above it, so the pressure there is biggest and the water is pushed out fastest.
build.commonError: Thinking all three jets are the same because it is the same water.

build.imageDescription: straight-line graph of pressure against depth in a lake, 100 kPa at the surface rising to 600 kPa at 50 m

questions.q: What is the pressure at 20 m deep?
questions.a: 300 kPa

questions.q: At what depth is the pressure 450 kPa?
The pressure at the surface is not zero. Why?
questions.a: The air above the lake presses on the water: air pressure is about 100 kPa.

developing.q: Plot a line graph of pressure (y-axis) against depth (x-axis) using the data table.
developing.a: A straight line from (0, 0) up to (10 000 m, 1000 atm).

developing.q: What happens to the pressure in water as you go deeper?
In which directions does water push on a diver?

reaching.q: Mark these on your graph: spider crab 300 m, blobfish 1200 m, vampire squid 3000 m, fangtooth 5000 m.
reaching.a: Four points on the line at 300, 1200, 3000 and 5000 m.

reaching.q: Explain why water pressure increases with depth.
reaching.a: Deeper down there is more water above. Its weight pushes down on the water below.
starters: Deeper down there is more water

reaching.q: Why is a dam built thicker at the bottom than at the top?
reaching.a: Water pressure is biggest at the bottom, so the wall must be strongest there.

mastering.q: Use your graph to find the pressure where each of the four animals lives. Which one withstands the most?
mastering.a: Spider crab 30, blobfish 120, vampire squid 300, fangtooth 500 atm. The fangtooth withstands the most.

mastering.q: A diver's ears hurt more at 10 m deep than at 2 m. Explain why.
mastering.a: At 10 m there is more water above, so the pressure pushing on the eardrum is bigger.

mastering.q: Submarines have thick, rounded hulls. Use ideas about pressure to explain why.
mastering.a: Deep water pressure is huge and pushes in all directions, so the hull must be strong all the way round or it would be crushed.

objectives: Describe the Big Bang theory and the evidence for it
Explain the origin and features of the cosmic microwave background
Use Wien's law to link the CMB to the early universe

questions.q: State Hubble's law.
questions.a: The recession velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from us.

questions.q: H_0 = 2.3 × 10^-18 s^-1. Estimate the age of the universe in years.
Define one parsec.
questions.a: The distance at which a radius of 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond.

questions.q: A star's spectrum peaks at 500 nm. Calculate its surface temperature.
State the cosmological principle.
questions.a: On a large scale the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and the laws of physics are universal.

questions.q: Write the equation linking the energy of a photon to its wavelength.
questions.a: E = hc ÷ λ

engage.hook: In 1965 a radio antenna picked up a faint microwave hiss from every direction in the sky. Pigeon droppings were blamed first.
engage.imageDescription: Holmdel horn antenna used by Penzias and Wilson in 1965

reveal.question: What was the hiss really?
reveal.answer: Radiation left over from the hot early universe, stretched into microwaves by expansion. It won Penzias and Wilson the 1978 Nobel Prize.

learn.heading: The Big Bang theory

items: About 13.7 billion years ago the universe began from an extremely hot, dense state.
Space itself has been expanding ever since.
As it expanded, the universe cooled.
Not an explosion into empty space: space itself stretches.
There is no centre. Every galaxy sees the others moving away.

learn.imageDescription: balloon with dots drawn on it being inflated, model of expanding space

rows.a: Expanding, so it was hotter and denser in the past
rows.b: Expanding, but new matter forms so density stays the same

rows.a: Predicts a cooled background radiation from the hot past

rows.b: Distant galaxies should look the same as near ones

rows.a: Supported by the CMB, found in 1965
rows.b: Abandoned after the CMB was found

learn.heading: The cosmic microwave background (CMB)

items: Microwave radiation from every direction in the sky.
A black-body spectrum peaking at about 1 mm, matching 2.7 K.
Almost isotropic: it varies by only about 1 part in 100 000.
About 380 000 years after the Big Bang, at about 3000 K, atoms formed.
Photons could then travel freely through space.
Expansion has since stretched their wavelength about 1100 times.

learn.imageDescription: black-body spectrum of the cosmic microwave background peaking at about 1.1 mm

build.q: Which observation is evidence that the universe is expanding?
options: Galaxies are red-shifted more the further away they are
Galaxies are blue-shifted more the further away they are
All stars have the same luminosity
build.explanation: Red shift increasing with distance means recession velocity is proportional to distance: expansion.

build.q: Why is the CMB evidence for the Big Bang?
options: It is radiation left from a hot, dense early universe
It is emitted by the Milky Way
It proves the universe is not expanding
build.explanation: A uniform black-body background is the cooled radiation the Big Bang model predicts.

build.q: The CMB is a black body at 2.7 K. What is its peak wavelength? (Wien constant = 2.9 × 10^-3 m K)
build.explanation: λ_max = 2.9 × 10^-3 ÷ 2.7 = 1.1 × 10^-3 m, about 1 mm: microwaves.

build.q: Which part of the EM spectrum is the CMB in today?
build.explanation: Its peak is near 1 mm, in the microwave region.

build.q: Why does the CMB arrive from every direction?
options: Earth is at the centre of the universe
It is reflected by the Milky Way
It was released everywhere in space at once
It is emitted by every star
build.explanation: It filled all of space when atoms formed, so it reaches us from everywhere.

build.q: Which observation could the steady-state model NOT explain?
options: The CMB and its black-body spectrum
build.explanation: Steady state has no hot dense past, so it predicts no CMB.

worked.prompt: The CMB was released at about 3000 K. Calculate its peak wavelength then. (Wien constant = 2.9 × 10^-3 m K)

yourTurn.prompt: Today the CMB peaks at 1.07 × 10^-3 m. By what factor have its wavelengths been stretched?

statements.text: The Big Bang was an explosion at one point in space.
statements.correction: Space itself expanded everywhere at once. There is no centre.

statements.text: The CMB is radiation from distant stars.
statements.correction: It was released about 380 000 years after the Big Bang, before any stars formed.

statements.text: The universe has cooled as it expanded.
The CMB is exactly the same in every direction.
statements.correction: It varies by about 1 part in 100 000. These ripples seeded galaxies.

developing.a: The universe began about 13.7 billion years ago from a very hot, dense state. Space has expanded and cooled ever since.

developing.q: State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory.
developing.a: Red shift of galaxies increasing with distance (expansion). The cosmic microwave background radiation.

developing.q: State two properties of the CMB.
developing.a: Black-body spectrum at 2.7 K with a peak near 1 mm (microwave). Almost the same in every direction (isotropic).

reaching.q: The CMB temperature is 2.7 K. Calculate its peak wavelength. (Wien constant = 2.9 × 10^-3 m K)
Explain how the CMB was produced and why it is now microwave radiation.
reaching.a: Released at about 3000 K when atoms formed. Expansion of space has since stretched its wavelength about 1100 times into microwaves.

reaching.q: Explain why the CMB is evidence against the steady-state model.
reaching.a: Steady state has no hot, dense past, so it predicts no black-body background. The CMB exists, as the Big Bang predicts.

mastering.q: The CMB peaks at 1.07 mm today. It was released at 3000 K. By what factor have its wavelengths stretched?
The CMB temperature varies by about 1 part in 100 000. Suggest why these tiny variations matter.
mastering.a: They show slightly denser regions in the early universe. Gravity pulled these together to form galaxies.

mastering.q: Evaluate the evidence that the universe began in a Big Bang.
mastering.a: Red shift rises with distance: expansion, so a denser past. CMB: a uniform 2.7 K black body, the cooled afterglow. Age from 1/H_0 fits the oldest stars.

objectives: Describe the difference between unicellular and multicellular organisms
Explain why large organisms need organs to absorb substances

questions.q: What does MRS GREN stand for?
questions.a: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition.

questions.q: Name the part of a cell that controls what the cell does.
questions.a: The nucleus.

questions.q: Name two parts found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
questions.a: Any two: cell wall, chloroplasts, permanent vacuole.

questions.q: What is a tissue?
questions.a: A group of similar cells working together to do a job.
questions.hint: A group of s_______ cells working t_______ to do a j_______.

questions.q: Name one specialised cell and say how it is adapted to its job.
questions.a: e.g. red blood cell: no nucleus, so more room to carry oxygen. Root hair cell: long hair, big surface to absorb water.

questions.q: Name the force that slows down a falling parachutist.
questions.a: Air resistance (drag).

engage.hook: A hungry alien can only eat living things made of ONE cell. Which of these could it eat?
engage.content: humans, cows, oak trees, ants, head lice, slugs, grass, mushrooms, tadpoles, moss, bacteria, amoeba
engage.imageDescription: cartoon pink alien with big eyes

reveal.answer: Only the bacteria and the amoeba. Everything else on the list is made of many cells, even the moss and the mushrooms.

rows.a: The one cell carries out all seven life processes
rows.b: Cells are specialised to do different jobs
Cells form tissues, organs and organ systems

rows.a: Usually too small to see without a microscope

learn.heading: The amoeba: one cell that does everything

items: It pushes out pseudopodia ("false feet") to move.
Pseudopodia surround food and take it into the cell.
A contractile vacuole collects extra water and squeezes it out.
Oxygen passes straight in through the cell membrane.

learn.imageDescription: amoeba under a microscope with pseudopodia, nucleus and contractile vacuole labelled

learn.heading: Why big organisms need organs

items: Substances only travel a short way to reach the middle of the cell.
The cell membrane can take in enough oxygen and food.
Cells deep inside are far from the surface.
Organs like lungs and intestines take in oxygen and food.
The blood carries them to every cell.

learn.imageDescription: particles outside a cell before and after moving into it through the membrane

build.q: What is a unicellular organism?
options: An organism made of many cells
An organism made of one cell
build.explanation: Uni means one: a unicellular organism is a single cell.

build.q: Which of these is multicellular?
build.explanation: A mushroom is made of many cells. The others are single cells.

build.q: How does an amoeba move?
build.explanation: Pseudopodia are "false feet" that let the cell creep along.

build.q: What do the agar cubes model?
build.explanation: Small cubes model small organisms. Big cubes model big organisms.

build.q: Which cube will turn colourless first?
options: They all change at the same time
build.explanation: The acid has the shortest distance to travel to reach the middle.

build.q: Why does a large organism need lungs and intestines?
options: Its middle is too far from the surface
It needs to make more cells
build.explanation: Inner cells are too far from the surface, so organs take in what they need.

build.title: Modelling organisms with agar cubes
build.intro: Pink agar cubes model organisms of different sizes. Acid soaking in turns them colourless.
equipment: pink agar cubes: 1 cm and 1.5 cm
steps: Use forceps to put each cube in its own beaker.
Pour acid over the cubes until they are covered. Start the stopwatch.
Record the time each cube takes to turn completely colourless.
Compare the times for the small and the large cubes.
build.warning: Eye protection on. Acid is an irritant: wash skin if splashed. Never eat the cubes.
build.imageDescription: beakers of acid with pink agar cubes of different sizes losing their colour

questions.q: Which cube turned colourless first? Why?
questions.a: The smallest. The acid had a shorter distance to travel to reach its middle.

questions.q: What does the large cube model?
questions.a: A large multicellular organism, whose middle is far from its surface.

developing.q: Sort into unicellular and multicellular: human, amoeba, oak tree, bacterium, ant, moss.
developing.a: Unicellular: amoeba, bacterium. Multicellular: human, oak tree, ant, moss.

developing.q: What does the word unicellular mean?
Name two life processes that an amoeba carries out in its one cell.
developing.a: Any two: movement, nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth, reproduction, sensitivity.

reaching.q: Describe two differences between unicellular and multicellular organisms.
reaching.a: Unicellular: one cell, no organs. Multicellular: many specialised cells forming tissues and organs.

reaching.q: Explain how an amoeba is adapted to catch food.
reaching.a: It pushes out pseudopodia that surround the food and take it into the cell.

reaching.q: In your experiment, which cube changed colour fastest? Explain why.
reaching.a: The smallest. The acid only had a short distance to travel to reach its middle.
starters: The cube that changed fastest was

mastering.q: Use your results to explain why large organisms need organs like lungs to take in oxygen.
mastering.a: In a big organism, inner cells are far from the surface, so oxygen would take too long to reach them. Lungs take it in and blood carries it.
starters: In the large cube, the acid
A large organism is like this because

mastering.q: A blue whale is made of trillions of cells. Why can it not take in oxygen through its skin like an amoeba?
mastering.a: Its inner cells are too far from the skin. Oxygen would take far too long to reach them, so it needs lungs and blood.

mastering.q: Give one advantage of being multicellular.
mastering.a: Cells can specialise, so the organism can grow larger and do more complex jobs. Losing one cell is not fatal.
